title: Women rabbis
hookLine: Reform ordains a woman in 1972, Reconstructionist in 1974, Conservative in 1985; Orthodox communities debate women's roles

lines: THEY ASK A QUESTION OF THE LAW.
cards: Five sisters walk up to Moses, in front of the priest, the leaders and the whole congregation: Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, the daughters of Zelophehad.

Their father has died with no sons, and with no son to inherit, his name and his share of the land will be lost to the family. They ask: why should our father's name be done away? Give us a possession.
Moses doesn't answer on his own. He brings their case before God, and the answer comes back: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right." A new law of inheritance follows.
Women standing up in front of everyone, asking the tradition a question.

teach.b: At the end of the same chapter, Moses hands leadership to Joshua. "And he laid his hands upon him, and gave him a charge." That laying on of hands is called semikhah, the word Jews still use for rabbinic ordination.
For a long time, only men received it. Then the movements of modern Judaism each faced the sisters' kind of question, in their own time and their own way.
Reform Judaism ordained a woman rabbi in 1972, the Reconstructionist movement in 1974, and the Conservative movement, after a long debate over Jewish law, in 1985.
Each decision came with arguments from the sources, and people on more than one side. In Orthodox communities the question is still open, and argued with real seriousness.
Some Orthodox institutions now train women in Jewish law and give them roles with new titles: teaching, answering questions, serving congregations.
Other Orthodox authorities hold that the rabbinate belongs to men, and that women's leadership should take other forms.
Both sides argue from the same Talmud, the same codes, the same respect for the law. So this isn't a story with a finish line.
It's how Jewish law moves: someone asks, the community argues, sometimes the answer changes and sometimes it doesn't, and the question stays open to the next person who asks.

how: Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative seminaries ordain women as rabbis and cantors; in Orthodox communities some institutions train women for teaching and advisory roles under new titles, while other Orthodox authorities hold that the rabbinate is for men.

games.q: you're one of the daughters of Zelophehad. your father has died with no sons, and his land will leave the family. what do you do?
o: go before Moses and the whole congregation and ask.
games.why: they asked in public. Moses brought their case before God, and the answer was "the daughters of Zelophehad speak right."

practice: Choose a community whose practice differs from yours, a synagogue, a church, a mosque, a family down the street, and instead of arguing with it in your head, try to name what it is protecting, what it loves, what it's afraid of losing.
Think of the five sisters and of Moses: a question asked in public, and an answer that took time. Let the difference sit without needing to settle it.

wordCard.voice: Women rabbis. Ordained in the Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative movements, and still debated, seriously and from the sources, in Orthodox communities. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: laying on of hands, from Moses and Joshua, and the word for rabbinic ordination.

carryVoice: Your line: the debates continue. Asking out loud is part of the law's life. Talk soon.
